Harmonizing the column names is the easy half of comparing EAVS years. The hard
half is that a jurisdiction's answer can change because its practice changed,
because the question changed, or because the way it answered changed, and the
panel looks identical in all three cases. `eavs_flags()` is how you tell them
apart, and on a multi-year panel it is not optional.


``` r
library(tidyeavs)

panel <- eavs_load(c(2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024), quiet = TRUE)
flags <- suppressMessages(eavs_flags(panel))
nrow(flags)
#> [1] 16249
```

That is a lot of flags, so the first job is triage rather than reading.

The messages suppressed above are worth seeing once: `eavs_flags()` reports how
many jurisdictions in each cycle had no counterpart in the previous one and so
could not be swing-checked. It is a handful per cycle, mostly genuinely new
jurisdictions. Jurisdictions are matched on a normalized code rather than the
published one, because a published code can change without the jurisdiction
changing, so this count is small on purpose.

## Three kinds, and they mean different things


``` r
table(flags$kind)
#> 
#> known_anomaly           sum         swing 
#>           171          3492         12586
```

A **sum** flag says subparts add up past their total. A **swing** flag says a
value moved implausibly against the same jurisdiction's previous cycle. A
**known_anomaly** flag says something no arithmetic can catch: a state answered
a question in a way that makes its value incomparable, verified against the
published file and recorded in `eavs_known_anomalies`.

None of these say a number is wrong. Thousands of independent jurisdictions keep
records differently, and most flags have ordinary explanations, which each
check's `note` spells out.

## Triage: filter to your concepts first

Nobody reads 16,000 flags. Filter to the concepts your analysis touches:


``` r
mine <- flags[flags$concept %in% c("mail_returned", "mail_rejected", "mail_counted"), ]
table(mine$check)
#> 
#>              dropped_to_zero                known_anomaly 
#>                           72                           72 
#> mail_disposition_le_returned         year_over_year_swing 
#>                          892                         3164
```

Then read the biggest ones within a kind. `excess` is a ballot count for sum
checks and a fold-change for swings, so it only sorts sensibly inside a kind:


``` r
worst <- mine[mine$kind == "sum", ]
head(worst[order(-worst$excess),
           c("year", "state_abbr", "jurisdiction_name", "check", "excess")], 5)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>    year state_abbr jurisdiction_name    check                        excess
#>   <dbl> <chr>      <chr>                <chr>                         <dbl>
#> 1  2018 CA         CONTRA COSTA COUNTY  mail_disposition_le_returned 124329
#> 2  2022 UT         WASHINGTON COUNTY    mail_disposition_le_returned  65664
#> 3  2018 IL         WILL COUNTY          mail_disposition_le_returned  24521
#> 4  2018 CA         SANTA CLARA COUNTY   mail_disposition_le_returned  22101
#> 5  2018 CA         SAN FRANCISCO COUNTY mail_disposition_le_returned  17547
```

## The flag that no arithmetic could have found

Oregon's 2018 mail numbers reconcile perfectly: counted plus rejected is
comfortably under returned. They are still unusable, because both figures cover
a small subset of ballots:


``` r
or <- subset(panel, state_abbr == "OR" & year %in% c(2016, 2018, 2020))
aggregate(cbind(mail_returned, mail_counted, mail_rejected) ~ year,
          data = or, FUN = sum, na.rm = TRUE, na.action = na.pass)
#>   year mail_returned mail_counted mail_rejected
#> 1 2016       2051452      2033878         17574
#> 2 2018       1907342         7043           176
#> 3 2020       2397091      2379544         17547
```

Counted collapses from about 2.0 million to 7,043 and back again, with returned
barely moving. A rejection rate built on 2018 would read near zero. Coverage
cannot see this, because every Oregon county answered; only knowing the
convention helps:


``` r
ka <- flags[flags$kind == "known_anomaly", ]
unique(ka[, c("year", "state_abbr", "concept")])
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>    year state_abbr concept          
#>   <dbl> <chr>      <chr>            
#> 1  2018 IA         polling_places_ed
#> 2  2018 OR         mail_counted     
#> 3  2018 OR         mail_rejected
cat(strwrap(unique(ka$note)[1], 78), sep = "\n")
#> All 99 Iowa counties report this item exactly equal to their Election Day
#> in-person voters (F1b), county by county, putting the 2018 national total
#> near 1.02M against 95k-107k in every other cycle. The state's 2018
#> polling-place counts are not comparable to its other years or to other
#> states.
```

Treat a `known_anomaly` row as a stop sign for that state-year, and read the
`source` column of `eavs_known_anomalies` if you want the evidence.

## Swings, and why they are noisy on purpose

The swing check flags a fold-change past `swing_factor` (10 by default) with both
cycles above `swing_floor` (100). It is deliberately blunt, and it fires on
ordinary things:


``` r
sw <- flags[flags$check == "year_over_year_swing", ]
head(sort(table(sw$concept), decreasing = TRUE), 5)
#> 
#>           mail_counted       mail_transmitted         partic_by_mail 
#>                   1587                   1503                   1441 
#>          mail_returned reg_confirmations_sent 
#>                   1384                    787
```

Mail items dominate, and they should: between 2016 and 2024 this panel spans the
2020 surge in mail voting and the partial reversion after it, which really did
move many jurisdictions by more than tenfold. `reg_confirmations_sent` is lumpy
for a different and equally ordinary reason, since list-maintenance mailings run
on a multi-year cycle rather than every election. Neither pattern is a data
problem. If your concept sits high on that list, raise the threshold rather than
reading every row:


``` r
tight <- suppressMessages(
  eavs_flags(panel, checks = NULL, anomalies = NULL, swing_factor = 50)
)
nrow(tight)
#> [1] 3189
```

A `dropped_to_zero` flag is split out separately, because a fall to zero would
otherwise be an infinite fold-change and would sort above every finite swing.
It is also the flag most likely to mean "the item went unreported this cycle"
rather than "the count really became zero", so check the reason before treating
it as a change.

## Concepts that do not exist in every year

Some items were only ever asked in some cycles. Drop boxes are the clean example:


``` r
eavs_items("drop_boxes_total")[, c("year", "code")]
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>    year code 
#>   <int> <chr>
#> 1  2016 <NA> 
#> 2  2018 <NA> 
#> 3  2020 <NA> 
#> 4  2022 C3a  
#> 5  2024 C3a
```

The panel carries `NA` for 2016 through 2020, which is correct but easy to
mistake for nonresponse. If you pass a status frame to `eavs_aggregate()`, those
rows land in `n_not_collected` rather than `n_missing`, and coverage for that
year is `NA` rather than zero, so "never asked" and "asked and unanswered" stay
distinguishable. See `vignette("missingness")`.

## A short checklist

Run `eavs_flags()` on the panel, not on a subset you have already narrowed.
Filter to your concepts, then sort within a kind. Treat known anomalies as
disqualifying for that state-year. Check `eavs_items()` for any concept whose
series looks discontinuous, since the `note` column usually explains it. And
prefer rates over levels when coverage moves between cycles, because a level can
change simply because more jurisdictions answered.
